title: GraphUniverse: Synthetic Graph Generation for Evaluating Inductive Generalization
claim: A generator composes a shared pool of semantic components, a family-level parameter ranges, and stepwise sampling to produce many consistent instances.
layout: 3 colored panels left-to-right, nested numbered steps, stacked graph-sample cards
description: A wide three-panel figure, read left to right. The left yellow UNIVERSE panel lists shared components. These are K colored community markers, a grayscale edge-propensity matrix, a degree-propensity vector, and feature-distribution cluster means and variances. The middle pink FAMILY panel shows the number of graphs g and six range sliders. They cover homophily, degree, node count, communities per graph, degree separation and power-law exponent. The right green GRAPH SAMPLE panel is drawn as stacked cards with a '...g' ellipsis, which implies many samples. It holds four numbered steps. Steps 1 and 2 sample the family parameters and select communities. Step 3 shows matrices that are subsampled and scaled into a red probability matrix. Step 4 generates the graph through node initialization, degree-factor assignment, edge generation and feature generation. The eye goes first to the colored community dots and the matrices.
caption: Overview of GraphUniverse generation methodology.
abstract: A fundamental challenge in graph learning is understanding how models generalize to new, unseen graphs. While synthetic benchmarks offer controlled settings for analysis, existing approaches are confined to single-graph, transductive settings where models train and test on the same graph structure. Addressing this gap, we introduce GraphUniverse, a framework for generating entire families of graphs to enable the first systematic evaluation of inductive generalization at scale. Our core innovation is the generation of graphs with persistent semantic communities, ensuring conceptual consistency while allowing fine-grained control over structural properties like homophily and degree distributions. This enables crucial but underexplored robustness tests, such as performance under controlled distribution shifts. Benchmarking a wide range of architectures -- from GNNs to graph transformers and topological architectures -- reveals that strong transductive performance is a poor predictor of inductive generalization. Furthermore, we find that robustness to distribution shift is highly sensitive not only to model architecture choice but also to the initial graph regime (e.g., high vs. low homophily). Beyond benchmarking, GraphUniverse's flexibility and scalability can facilitate the development of robust and truly generalizable architectures. The framework is open-source at https://github.com/LouisVanLangendonck/GraphUniverse.
